text: Ghana, officially the Republic of Ghana, is a country in West Africa located along the Gulf of Guinea and the Atlantic Ocean, sharing borders with Côte d'Ivoire to the west, Burkina Faso to the north, and Togo to the east. It covers an area of 239,567 km² (92,497 sq mi) and has an Atlantic coastline of about 560 kilometres (350 miles), situated between latitudes 4°45′N and 11°N and longitudes 1°15′E and 3°15′W. The Prime Meridian passes through Tema, near Accra, making Ghana the country closest to the intersection of the Prime Meridian and the Equator (0°, 0°). The country spans diverse ecologies, including coastal savannas, tropical rainforests, and grasslands mixed with shrublands and forests, with forest extending northward 320 kilometres (200 miles) and eastward up to 270 kilometres (170 miles). Ghana is home to five terrestrial ecoregions: Eastern Guinean forests, Guinean forest–savanna mosaic, West Sudanian savanna, Central African mangroves, and Guinean mangroves. The climate is tropical, featuring a wet and dry season, and Ghana lies at the intersection of three hydro-climatic zones—warm and dry in the east, hot and humid in the southwest, and hot and dry in the north. The White Volta River and its tributary, the Black Volta, flow south through Ghana to Lake Volta, the world’s third-largest reservoir by volume and largest by surface area, formed by the hydroelectric Akosombo Dam completed in 1965. The Volta exits Lake Volta into the Gulf of Guinea. The northernmost point is Pulmakong and the southernmost is Cape Three Points. With over 35 million inhabitants, Ghana is the thirteenth-most populous country in Africa and the second-most populous in West Africa. The capital and largest city is Accra. The earliest kingdoms to emerge in Ghana were Bonoman in the south and the Kingdom of Dagbon in the north, with Bonoman existing in the area during the 11th century. From the 17th century, different Akan states emerged from the Bonoman area, primarily based on gold trading, including Bonoman (Brong-Ahafo), Adansi and Asante (Ashanti), Denkyira, Mankessim, Akyem, and Akwamu. By the 19th century, the southern part of Ghana was included in the Asante Kingdom, which developed from a loose network into a centralized kingdom with a specialized bureaucracy based in Kumasi. Prior to European contact, the Akan people developed an economy centered on gold and gold bars traded with other African states. European contact began with the Portuguese in the 15th century, who established the Portuguese Gold Coast (Costa do Ouro) and built a trading lodge at Anomansah, renamed São Jorge da Mina, with Elmina Castle commissioned in 1481 and completed in three years. By 1598, the Dutch joined the trade, establishing the Dutch Gold Coast and building forts at Fort Komenda and Kormantsi, capturing Elmina Castle in 1617 and Fort St Anthony in 1642. Other European powers, including the Swedes, Danes, and Germans, established their own Gold Coast territories, with the Germans building the Brandenburger Gold Coast or Groß Friedrichsburg. By 1874, Great Britain established control over parts of the country, assigning them the status of the British Gold Coast. Military conflicts between British colonial forces and Akan states, including the Anglo-Ashanti wars, culminated in the War of the Golden Stool in 1900, after which the Ashanti lost control. In the late 19th century, cocoa cultivation expanded through the tropical forests, supported by the British administration. In 1947, the United Gold Coast Convention, led by "The Big Six," called for self-government within the shortest possible time following the 1946 legislative election. Kwame Nkrumah, who led Ghana from 1957 to 1966 as its first prime minister and president, formed the Convention People's Party in 1949 with the motto "self-government now" and initiated a "positive action" campaign involving non-violent protests, strikes, and non-cooperation with British authorities. Nkrumah was arrested and sentenced to one year in prison, released after being elected to Parliament in the 1951 general election, and became prime minister in 1952, implementing a policy of Africanization. On 6 March 1957, the Gold Coast, Ashanti, the Northern Territories, and British Togoland were unified as an independent dominion within the British Commonwealth under the Ghana Independence Act 1957, adopting the name Ghana. The current flag, consisting of red, gold, green, and a black star, dates from this unification. On 1 July 1960, following a constitutional referendum and presidential election, Nkrumah declared Ghana a republic and assumed the presidency. 6 March is celebrated as Independence Day and 1 July as Republic Day. Nkrumah led an authoritarian regime, repressing political opposition and conducting non-free and non-fair elections. In 1964, a constitutional amendment made Ghana a one-party state with Nkrumah as president for life. He was the first African head of state to promote Pan-Africanism, merging teachings from Marcus Garvey, Martin Luther King Jr., and W. E. B. Du Bois, and played a key role in founding the Non-Aligned Movement and establishing the Kwame Nkrumah Ideological Institute to teach his ideologies of communism and socialism. His centenary was celebrated as a public holiday, known as Founders' Day. In 1966, a military coup codenamed "Operation Cold Chop" overthrew Nkrumah while he was in China, led by Colonel Emmanuel Kwasi Kotoka and Brigadier Akwasi Afrifa, forming the National Liberation Council chaired by Lieutenant General Joseph A. Ankrah. From 1966, Ghana was ruled by alternating military and civilian governments, often affected by economic instability, ending with Flight Lieutenant Jerry John Rawlings of the Provisional National Defence Council coming to power in 1981. In 1981, the constitution was suspended and political parties banned. Rawlings negotiated a structural adjustment plan, leading to economic recovery in the mid-1980s. A new constitution restoring multi-party politics was introduced in the 1992 presidential election, in which Rawlings was elected and again in the 1996 general election. In 1994, a tribal war in Northern Ghana between the Konkomba and other ethnic groups, including the Nanumba, Dagomba, and Gonja, resulted in between 1,000 and 2,000 deaths and 150,000 displacements. After the 2000 general election, John Kufuor of the New Patriotic Party became president on 7 January 2001 and was re-elected in 2004, marking the first peaceful transfer of power under the fourth republic. In the 2008 general election, Nana Akufo-Addo was defeated by John Atta Mills of the National Democratic Congress. Mills died of natural causes and was succeeded by Vice President John Mahama on 24 July 2012. Following the 2012 general election, Mahama became president in his own right, and Ghana was described as a "stable democracy." After the 2016 general election, Nana Akufo-Addo became president on 7 January 2017 and was re-elected in 2020. Akufo-Addo’s presidency ended in January 2025, and John Mahama succeeded him as president. To combat deforestation, on 11 June 2021, Ghana inaugurated Green Ghana Day with the goal of planting five million trees. On 6 August 2025, shortly after takeoff at Kotoka International Airport, a Harbin Z-9 crashed into a forested mountainside, killing eight people, including ministers Edward Omane Boamah and Ibrahim Murtala Muhammed. Ghana declared three days of mourning on 7 August and held a state funeral on 15 August at Black Star Square in Accra. Ghana is a multi-ethnic country with diverse linguistic and religious groups; the Akan are the largest ethnic group but constitute a plurality. Most Ghanaians are Christians (71.3%), nearly a fifth are Muslims, and a tenth practice traditional faiths or report no religion. Ghana is a unitary constitutional democracy led by a president who serves as both head of state and head of government. It ranked seventh in the 2022 Ibrahim Index of African Governance and fifth in the 2024 Fragile States Index. Since 1993, it has maintained one of the freest and most stable governments on the continent, performing well in healthcare, economic growth, and human development. Ghana has significant influence in West Africa and across Africa as a whole. It is a founding member of the Non-Aligned Movement and the African Union, and a member of the United Nations, South Atlantic Peace and Cooperation Zone, Economic Community of West African States, the Group of 24, and the Commonwealth of Nations. The name Ghana originates from Wagadu, a West African empire from the 3rd to 12th centuries, which Arab traders referred to as Ghana, derived from the title Kaya Maghan, meaning "ruler of gold." Rev. J. B. Anaman proposed a historical connection between the peoples of the Gold Coast and ancient Ghana in the early 20th century, drawing on D. W. Cooley’s interpretations of Arabic sources, and suggested an alternative derivation from the Wangara. Lady Flora Shaw compiled Arabic and European writings to present the kingdom as a major African power comparable to contemporary Western European states. Between 1907 and 1911, Rev. W. T. Balmer promoted the theory that the Akan peoples migrated from the medieval Empire of Ghana, a hypothesis later supported by Jack Goody, who noted it lacked linguistic and historical evidence but became influential among educated elites and nationalist intellectuals. The theory gained popularity in the 1920s in educational institutions, especially at Achimota, and was publicized by J. B. Danquah, who used Arabic and French translations to claim the Akan migrated from the Upper Niger region and associated the name Ghana with Akane or Akana, linking it to the ancient region of Akkad. Eva L. R. Meyerowitz expanded this narrative, claiming Akan origins and culture came from the Sahara and the Near East, suggesting Akan culture was Libya-Berber or connected to Mediterranean or Near Eastern cultures. By the time of independence, the name "Ghana" was widely accepted as a symbol of precolonial prestige, cultural unity, and national legitimacy. Ghana signed the Paris Agreement in 2016 and aims to avoid 64 million metric tons of greenhouse gas emissions by 2030. Climate change is having significant impacts, with increasing temperatures, changing rainfall, extreme weather, drought, wildfires, floods, and sea-level rise expected to negatively affect infrastructure, hydropower, food security, water supply, and coastal and agricultural livelihoods. Diseases such as malaria, dengue fever, and cholera are predicted to increase due to changes in water conditions.
